questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ){|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =4([0-1]-[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]) \\  & =4(\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$  

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi /2)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=6$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(6)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 6\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =3({(3\sqrt{3})}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 27 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $y=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$, where $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
